en: The Nādabindūpaniṣad: Oṃ.
The letter *a* is the right wing, while the letter *u* is remembered as the left;
the letter *m* is its tail, and the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) is likewise its head.
His feet are said to be *rajas* and *tamas*, and his body is *sattva*;
righteousness (*dharma*) is remembered as his right eye, and unrighteousness (*adharma*) as his left.
The *bhūr* world is in his feet, the *bhuvar* world is in his knees,
the *svar* world is in the region of his hips, and the *mahar* world is in the region of his navel.
Janaloka is in the heart; from there, Tapas is in the region of the throat;
and Satyaloka is situated between the eyebrows and the middle of the forehead.
And here, the mantra "A thousandfold" has been shown;
thus the one skilled in yoga, having mounted this *haṃsa*, [proceeds].
The practitioner of action is not bound even by hundreds of millions of evils;
this first measure belongs to Agni, and it follows the will of Vāyu.
The subsequent measure should be like the orb of the sun;
the supreme half-measure, the wise know that to be Vāruṇī.
Or else, it has three parts and faces, and their foundation is established in the measures (mātrās).
This is declared to be the syllable Oṃ; learn [it] through the meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās). NbiUp_8 //
Yoṣiṇī is the first measure, Vidyunmālā is the next;
Pataṅgī shall be the third, and Vāyuveginī the fourth.
The fifth is prescribed as Ādheyā, and the sixth is ordained as Aindrī;
the seventh is named Vaiṣṇavī, and the eighth is likewise Śaṃkarī.
The ninth is named Mahatī; the tenth is considered Dhruvā;
the eleventh shall be Maunī; and the twelfth is considered Brāhmī.
If one is separated from the vital breaths during the first measure,
he is born as a sovereign emperor over the whole of Bhārata-varṣa.
On the second [day], he who has passed away becomes a high-souled yakṣa;
on the third, a vidyādhara; and on the fourth, a gandharva.
Now, if one is separated from the vital breaths during the fifth measure,
having dwelt as a companion of the gods, he is glorified in the world of Soma.
In the sixth [state] one attains union with Indra; in the seventh, the station of Viṣṇu;
and in the eighth, one goes to Rudra, the Lord of Creatures.
On the ninth [day] one goes to Maharloka, and on the tenth to Dhruvaloka;
on the eleventh to Tapoloka, and on the twelfth to the eternal Brahman.
Beyond that is the supreme Brahman— pure, all-pervading, partless, auspicious, and eternally manifest— from which the rising of all lights proceeds.

When the mind becomes beyond the senses, transcends the qualities (guṇas), and is absorbed in stillness, one should then declare it to be united with yoga— beyond comparison and free from objective existence.
Devoted to that and absorbed in that,
well-established through the practice of yoga and free from all attachments, he shall gradually cast off the body.
Then, with his bonds dissolved, he becomes the stainless, absolute Lord;
by that very state of Brahman, he enjoys supreme bliss.
